name: Sendai Airport
before:
The largest airport in the Tōhoku region, at Natori about 13.6 km south south east of Sendai. It carries around 3.6 million passengers a year, which puts it roughly tenth in Japan.

The rail link makes it easy. The Sendai Airport Line opened in March 2007 and runs to Sendai Station in 17 to 25 minutes. By road it is reached on the Sendai Tōbu Road, with two car parks holding 970 and 250 spaces.

The terminal has four levels and eight jet bridges, with domestic flights at the west end and international at the east. Arrivals and baggage reclaim are on the ground floor, departures on the second, and the third has shops, a business lounge and an observation deck. It was designed by Gyo Obata of Hellmuth, Obata and Kassabaum.

The airport was badly damaged by the earthquake and tsunami of 2011, and the railway into the city did not reopen until that October. It began life in 1940 as an army flight training field.
after:
The largest airport in the Tōhoku region, at Natori about 14 km south south east of Sendai. It handled just over 4 million passengers in the year to March 2026.

The rail link makes it easy. Opened in 2007, the Sendai Airport Line runs to Sendai Station in 17 to 25 minutes.

Domestic and international flights share one terminal, with arrivals on the ground floor and departures on the second. The airport is refitting its second and third floors until March 2029 and warns that some facilities will be closed or restricted while the work goes on.

It was badly damaged by the earthquake and tsunami of 2011.

claims.claim: the largest airport in the Tōhoku region
claims.inAfter: The largest airport in the Tōhoku region
claims.note: The Tokyo Civil Aviation Bureau's table covers every airport in its area, Tōhoku included. For January to July 2026 Sendai handled 2,276,899 of the 4,875,650 passengers at the region's nine airports (47 per cent), and no other Tōhoku row passes 750,000. The rows were matched to names with care, because the PDF prints the names apart from the figures: Sendai's row is the first after the zero-filled regional total, as in the page's name order (丘珠, 仙台, 秋田, 山形), and the nine Tōhoku rows for January (310,815 for Sendai, 85,294, 25,697, 81,424, 32,892, 13,687, 23,445, 20,429 and 29,407) add up exactly to the regional January total of 623,090. The operator calls Sendai Tōhoku's air gateway in its March 2026 notice.

claims.inAfter: It handled just over 4 million passengers in the year to March 2026.
claims.note: Was 'around 3.6 million passengers a year'. For the 2025 financial year (April 2025 to March 2026) the operator's preliminary count, its own tally from the airlines' figures, is 4,000,689 and MLIT's sheet has 4,031,331. Both give 661,378 international passengers, which ties MLIT's row to Sendai; the domestic counts differ by about 30,600. The operator's figure for the year before (3,778,423) is the one Wikipedia's infobox gives for 2024.

claims.claim: the airport is refitting its second and third floors until March 2029 and warns some facilities will be closed or restricted
claims.inAfter: The airport is refitting its second and third floors until March 2029 and warns that some facilities will be closed or restricted while the work goes on.
claims.note: Replaces the floor-by-floor account of the upper floors ('the third has shops, a business lounge and an observation deck'), which the operator's current floor map no longer matches and which this work is changing. The operator's notice of 24 March 2026: the refit of floors 2 and 3, paused in November 2020 by the pandemic, restarted in March 2026 and is planned to finish, with a grand opening, in March 2029; it enlarges the shops on the second floor, fills the third floor with restaurants, extends both boarding lounges to the third floor and moves the card lounge to the domestic third floor after security. Attributed to the airport, as the plan and the warning are its own.

claims.claim: about 13.6 km
claims.wasBefore: about 13.6 km south south east of Sendai
claims.why: Rounded to about 14 km (see above): 13.6 km on Wikipedia, 14.8 km in a straight line on the coordinates.

claims.claim: around 3.6 million passengers a year
claims.wasBefore: It carries around 3.6 million passengers a year
claims.why: Out of date: the operator counted 3,778,423 for the year to March 2025 and 4,000,689 for the year to March 2026. Replaced by the latest year (see above).

claims.claim: roughly tenth in Japan
claims.wasBefore: which puts it roughly tenth in Japan
claims.why: A national ranking the operator does not state. MLIT's national ranking tables are Excel files the sweep's tools cannot save, and its readable sheets leave out the company-run airports (Narita, Kansai, Itami, Chubu), so no current rank could be confirmed.

claims.claim: opened in March 2007
claims.wasBefore: The Sendai Airport Line opened in March 2007
claims.why: Softened to 2007 (see above): the month rests on Wikipedia alone.

claims.claim: reached by road on the Sendai Tōbu Road
claims.wasBefore: By road it is reached on the Sendai Tōbu Road
claims.why: Wikipedia alone. The operator's car, parking and access FAQ pages (Japanese and English) name no road, and no other source was found in three tries.

claims.claim: two car parks of 970 and 250 spaces
claims.wasBefore: with two car parks holding 970 and 250 spaces
claims.why: Wikipedia alone. The operator's parking and access FAQ pages give no capacities, and its car parks are now signed 1R (reserved), 1A, 1B and 2.

claims.claim: four levels and eight jet bridges
claims.wasBefore: The terminal has four levels and eight jet bridges
claims.why: The floors are counted differently (Wikipedia: G1, M2, 2 and 3; the operator's floor map: 1F, 2F, 3F and the roof deck), and the eight jet bridges rest on Wikipedia alone. MLIT also records a new boarding pier opened in 2018 (平成30年 新旅客搭乗施設（ピア棟）供用開始), so the count may be out of date.

claims.claim: domestic at the west end, international at the east
claims.wasBefore: with domestic flights at the west end and international at the east
claims.why: Softened to one shared terminal (see above): the ends rest on Wikipedia alone.

claims.claim: baggage reclaim on the ground floor
claims.wasBefore: Arrivals and baggage reclaim are on the ground floor
claims.why: Arrivals on the ground floor are kept (see above); baggage reclaim there rests on Wikipedia alone.

claims.claim: the third floor has shops, a business lounge and an observation deck
claims.wasBefore: and the third has shops, a business lounge and an observation deck
claims.why: Partly out of date: the operator's floor map lists the shops on the first and second floors and restaurants on the third, and its roof, not the third floor, carries the observation deck ('RF 展望デッキ'). The third-floor business lounge is on the operator's map and Wikipedia, but the refit that runs to March 2029 is moving the lounges and shops, so the refit replaces the floor-by-floor detail (see above).

claims.claim: designed by Gyo Obata of HOK
claims.wasBefore: It was designed by Gyo Obata of Hellmuth, Obata and Kassabaum.
claims.why: Wikipedia alone. HOK's own aviation project lists (hok.com, read 2026-09-23) do not include Sendai, and the operator's history describes the 1997 terminal without naming an architect.

claims.claim: the railway did not reopen until October 2011
claims.wasBefore: and the railway into the city did not reopen until that October
claims.why: Wikipedia alone. The railway's company and 2026 safety report pages and the Tokyo Civil Aviation Bureau's Sendai page give no reopening date. The operator's history gives flights instead: temporary flights about a month after the disaster, domestic scheduled flights from July 2011 and international from September 2011.

claims.claim: began life in 1940 as an army flight training field
claims.wasBefore: It began life in 1940 as an army flight training field.
claims.why: Wikipedia alone. The operator's history starts in 1956, when GHQ returned the Yanome airfield, which opened the next year as Sendai Airfield and took the name Sendai Airport in 1964; it says nothing of 1940 or army training.

opinion.text: The rail link makes it easy.
opinion.why: Framing carried over from the old text. The operator says the station and terminal are directly connected with no steps (sia-access), and the railway runs through trains to Sendai Station without a change (senat-faq).
